blocks.text: It is proved that עטלף atalleph is the bat.

As Moses began with the eagle, which is the queen of birds, so he ended with the bat, which is of ambiguous nature and holds a middle place between birds and quadrupeds. To this belongs what the Philosopher writes, that it ἐπαμφοτερίζειν τοῖς πτηνοῖς καὶ πεζοῖς, ἀμφωτέρων τε μετέχειν, καὶ οὐδετέρων [epamphoterizein tois ptēnois kai pezois, amphōterōn te metechein, kai oudeterōn], On the Parts of Animals, book 4, chapter 13. Hence Varro in the Agathon:
In short? I have become a bat, and am plainly neither among the mice nor among the birds.

And Macrobius, Saturnalia, book 7, chapter 16: “From the beginning all flying creatures come forth from eggs, except one, which is of uncertain nature. For the bat does indeed fly on wings of skin; but it is not to be counted among flying creatures, because it walks on four feet, bears fully formed young, and nourishes with milk those it begets.” Therefore, just as the Samaritans in Josephus professed themselves now Jews, now gentiles, according as the affairs of the Jews went well or badly, so in the fables the bat declares itself now a mouse, now a bird, as suits its interest. And well known is the riddle of Panarces, ὅτι βάλοι ξύλῳ τε καὶ οὐ ξύλῳ καθημένην ὄρνιθα καὶ οὐκ ὄρνιθα ἀνήρ τε καὶ οὐκ ἀνὴρ λίθῳ καὶ οὐ λίθῳ [hoti baloi xylō te kai ou xylō kathēmenēn ornitha kai ouk ornitha anēr te kai ouk anēr lithō kai ou lithō], a man not a man (a eunuch) strikes a bird not a bird (a bat) sitting on wood not wood (a fennel stalk), with a stone [III, 116] not a stone (pumice). This riddle is mentioned by Plato in book 5 of the Laws, by Clearchus in his book On Riddles, by Athenaeus, book 10, chapter 19, and by Suidas in passing under Νυκτερίδος αἶνος [Nykteridos ainos]. A very learned man wonders why this bird is said there to sit, since it does not sit, but either flies or clings hanging from rocks or the branches of trees. He therefore wants καθημένην [kathēmenēn] changed to πετομένην [petomenēn]. But I do not think anything should be changed. Καθήμενος [Kathēmenos] does not always mean sitting, but often settled, remaining, resting. For examples see Matth. IV, 16. and IX, 9. and XI, 16. and elsewhere. The matter is too well known to need proof. And for the Romans too sedere [to sit] means exactly this. Thus of this same bird Symposius, Riddle 28:
But I sit in darkness, and do not entrust myself to the daylight. [col. 350]

Why it is called עטלף atalleph in Hebrew and עטלפא attallepha in Chaldee has hitherto been uncertain, but I shall try to disclose this unknown matter. In polysyllabic names one often sees transpositions of letters: as in אלגומים algumim for אלמוגים almugim; מתלעות mathleoth for מלתעות maltheoth; and in the Egyptian CALASIRI from קרסול karsol. I would think something similar happened here, and that עטלף atalleph was said for עפטלל aphtalel, or ephtalel, that is, bird of darkness. For עוף oph is bird; and the Hebrew צל tsel, or צלל tselal, for shadow and darkness, is written in Chaldee טול tul and טלל telall ^{(1)}. Thus this bird would have had a name plainly fitting its nature. For in Greek too it is called νυκτερὶς [nykteris] from ἀπὸ τῆς νυκτὸς [apo tēs nyktos], because it is ἐκ τῶν νυκτινόμων [ek tōn nyktinomōn]. Nor is the reason for the Roman name any different. Ovid, Metamorphoses, book 4, Fable 12:
They fly by night, and take their name from the late evening.
Symposius, in the place cited above:
Night gives me my name, from the first hour of the night.

Nonius: “The bat, a winged animal of two forms; so called because in the evening (vespere) it prepares itself for its night flight.” Isidore: “The bat received its name from the time, because, fleeing the light, it flies about in the evening twilight.” The Arabs call it الخغاش [al-khghāsh] alchopphas, from a defect of the eyes. Alcamus: الخغاش الوطواط سمي لصغر عينيه وضعف بصره [al-khghāsh al-waṭwāṭ summiya li-ṣighar ʿaynayhi wa-ḍaʿf baṣarihi] “Alchopphas is the same as alvvatvvat (bat). It is so called because of the smallness of its eyes and the weakness of its sight.” [III, 117] For الخفش [al-khafash] alchaphas is, according to the same author, صغر العين وضعف البصر خلقة او فصال في الجفون بلا وجع وان يبصر باليل دون النهار وفي يوم غيم دون صاحي [ṣighar al-ʿayn wa-ḍaʿf al-baṣar khilqatan aw fiṣāl fī al-jufūn bi-lā wajaʿ wa-an yubṣira bi-l-layl dūna al-nahār wa-fī yawm ghaym dūna ṣāḥī] “smallness of the eye and natural weakness of sight, or a defect in the eyelids without pain, or when someone sees better by night than by day, and on a cloudy day better than on a clear one.”

Outside the Law there is only one passage in Scripture that deals with the bat, namely Esa. II, 20. “In that day a man shall cast away his idols of silver and his idols of gold, which he had made for himself to worship, to the moles ולעטלפים, and to the bats”: that is, he will thrust them into darkness, so that they may no longer delude superstitious people with their glitter. For as the mole is blind, so the bat flees the light; this we have shown at greater length in the chapter On Moles ^{a)}.
